sentence: the protagonist of this one was a woman in her forties making bad decisions and the camera just stayed with her, no judgment, no music telling you what to feel. i miss this kind of filmmaking. i miss films that trust you. i miss films that don't pre-chew their emotions for you.

had the friendship crisis again. the one where i think nobody actually likes me and they're all just being nice. went to therapy. she said my brain is a liar. i know my brain is a liar. but knowing your brain is a liar doesn't actually stop it from lying. anyway. i'm fine. mostly. tomorrow will be better. hopefully.

there's a specific kind of pacing in low-budget movies where you can feel the editor's hand on every cut. they don't have enough coverage. they're making do. and i love this. it makes the film feel like it was made by hands instead of by a committee of agents.

a small / brown / dog / on a / red / leash / walking / past / and / the world / for one / second / is / only / this / and / nothing / else / matters / because / look / look / a dog / a brown / dog / and the / sun / is / out
in the small green hour before / morning / a bird is doing what / a bird does and / i am here / a body / breathing / and that / is / enough / it has to be / enough / it is / it is / it is

the courthouse in the middle of town has a clock that has been wrong for six years. it says 4:18. nobody fixes it. it has become a joke. it has become a landmark. people meet at the wrong clock. you tell visitors to meet at the wrong clock. the wrong clock is part of who we are now. don't try to fix it. we like it broken.

october / again / how / how / how / does it / keep / coming / back / and the trees / do their / quiet / undressing / and / i / stand / at / the / window / again / wondering / what / i did / with / last / year

polaroids cost more per frame than they should and that's also the point. you slow down. you think before you press. there is no 'just one more.' every photo is a decision. every photo is a small bet that this thing in front of you is worth a piece of plastic film.

i still buy stamps in person at the post office. the clerk knows me. she keeps the good ones aside. last week she gave me a set with old paintings on them. i used one to mail a card to my mother. my mother called me to say she loved the stamp. she didn't mention what i wrote in the card. she just talked about the stamp. that's love. that's love too.

a list for old houses. for creaky floors and slow plumbing. for windows that don't quite close. for porches and screen doors. for the smell of someone else's grandmother's kitchen. for being a guest in a town you used to live in. for being a ghost in your own old life.

the rain started around eleven this morning and hasn't stopped. the cat is mad about it. she keeps going to the door and looking outside and turning around in disgust. she does this every hour like she's expecting the weather to have changed. it has not. it is not going to. but i admire her persistence. i admire her refusal to accept the world as it is.

everyone in town drives a pickup or a subaru. there is no in between. you are one tribe or the other. you can switch tribes but you have to commit. you cannot drive a sedan. the sedan people don't come here. they don't last. the snow eats them by january. you have to commit to the truck or the subaru. those are the rules.

first dinner party tonight, sort of. just two friends. we sat on the floor with pizza because i don't have a table yet. it was one of the best nights of my life. there's a particular joy in inviting people into a space that's truly yours for the first time.

five years ago today i was in a hospital. i was twenty-eight pounds lighter. i did not think i would make it to thirty. now i am thirty-two. now i am running 5ks. now i am eating lunch every day. thank you to the people who stayed. you saved my life. i don't say that lightly.

i think the best part of a bus ride is when it's almost dark and the inside of the bus is dim and everyone is in their own little world with their headphones and their phones, and outside the world is doing its slow blue thing, and you feel like you're suspended between places.

i told my dad i wanted to be a writer when i grow up and he said writing is a fine hobby but i should pick a real job. i am not speaking to him for the rest of my life. or at least until tomorrow. i'm going to be a writer. i'm going to be famous. and then he'll be sorry. and then i won't even care.

the last night of camp every summer we lit a bonfire and everyone read a letter they had written to themselves at the start of the session. the letters were small. they were not profound. they were what an eleven-year-old or twelve-year-old or thirteen-year-old thought was important. and then we threw them into the fire. and the fire took them. and we cried. all of us. every year.

tea at 1am for no reason, just because the kettle was right there and i wanted to hold something warm. didn't even want to drink it really. just wanted the ritual. the scoop, the pour, the steam. i think a lot of life is making excuses to do small slow things that you don't strictly need to do.

my partner came home with flowers tonight. she said they reminded her of me. they were small and yellow and slightly crooked in the vase. and that's the most accurate thing anyone has ever said about how i present in this world. small and yellow and slightly crooked. i'm going to cry about this for like a week.

writing a letter is a kind of meditation. you sit down. you choose a pen. you put paper in front of you. you think about the person. you write to them slowly. you can't take it back. you can't delete. you have to mean what you say. you have to be patient with yourself. you have to let it be imperfect. it's the opposite of an email. it's the opposite of a text.

thursday. bad day. nothing happened. just the static kind of bad. couldn't focus at work. snapped at the dog for nothing. cried in the shower. ate cereal for dinner. some days are like this. tomorrow is allowed to be different. i'm going to bed now. trying not to be too hard on myself about it.

the apartment has too many plants. there. i said it. there are too many. i don't have room for furniture. i don't have room for guests. i keep buying more. i don't know why. there's something deeply broken in me that needs to keep buying ferns. my therapist says it's about control. i think it's about life. she didn't disagree.

glued an old library card next to a piece of an envelope my grandfather addressed in 1972. handwriting next to handwriting. two strangers' loops and slants in conversation across decades on my paper. this is what i'm making now. paper conversations between people who never met.

wednesday. saw my therapist. she said something that's been rattling around all day: that the people who hurt me weren't doing it because i deserved it, they were doing it because they were hurt. it doesn't fix anything. but it loosens something. i can feel it. like a knot starting to give.

people stop us on the street to comment on her size. she is used to it. i am used to it. it has stopped being a conversation. i just say yes she is small. yes she is fully grown. yes she is six pounds. and they say oh my god how cute. and they reach for her. and she lets them. she is the ambassador of small dogs everywhere. she is a small dog professional. she is the boss.

in seventh grade i was so in love with daniel that i would walk a longer way to class just to pass his locker. he didn't know my name until april. when he finally said hi to me in the hallway i could not respond. i just walked into the wall. i actually walked into the wall. he laughed. it was the best moment of my life so far.

found my grandmother's old embroidery scissors in a box of stuff my mom sent me. tiny stork-shaped ones, the beak is where you cut. they're still sharper than anything i own. i've been holding them all afternoon thinking about her hands. i don't even remember if she embroidered, but she had these.

checked out three novels and a biography and i know full well i'll only read one of them but the act of carrying them home in a tote bag feels important. they're a kind of promise. i could read them. they're available to me. the option of them is enough.

to the strangers at my brother's funeral who said the things i needed to hear: i don't remember your faces. i barely remember my own face from those weeks. but the words you said are still in my chest. you didn't have to. nobody had to. but you did. and i'm telling you, even though you'll never read this: thank you.

estate sale today. a woman who collected ceramic animals. i mean collected. there were hundreds. they were arranged on every surface of her house. her children were selling them in batches. i bought a small ceramic owl for two dollars. the owl is sitting on my desk now. it is judging me. i hope the woman would be okay with this. i hope the owl is happy here.

missed a week of training because of the flu. felt sorry for myself for six days. on the seventh day i went outside and ran a slow easy three miles and remembered why i do this. it's not about the goals. it's about the going outside. it's about the breath. the goals are just an excuse to keep going outside.

sometimes at 3am i think about how the moon has been watching everyone i've ever loved sleep and that feels like the most intimate thing in the world. like the moon knows my mother's face when she dreams. the moon knows what my exes look like with their guards down. it's the only witness to all of us.

a friend gave me her grandmother's sewing machine. it weighs forty pounds. it is from 1952. it still works. it is olive green and gold and it has the original manual. i don't know how to sew. i'm going to learn. i'm going to make small bad things on this machine. i'm going to keep my friend's grandmother in my life by making bad pillowcases.

the marina office has a free books cart and i have read more in three months than i did in the previous three years. mostly thrillers. occasionally a tide chart. once a self-help book i couldn't put down because the woman who donated it had written angry annotations in the margins, which were better than the book itself.

to the person who picked up my wallet on the bus last tuesday and turned it in to the driver with everything still inside: thank you. i don't know who you are. i don't know if i passed you on the street the next day. but you saved my week. you saved my month maybe. you are good. you are good and you should know it.

the porch swing creaks in a rhythm that's two beats slower than my breathing and i'm working on letting my breathing slow down to meet it instead of speeding it up. it's not a competition, the swing has been here longer, the swing knows the pace, i should follow her lead.

and the streetlights flickered on like they were waiting for me / and the wind picked up your name and carried it past me / and the night smelled like rain and nothing else mattered / and i walked home alone like that's something to be proud of / and maybe it is / and maybe it isn't

the dog who lives at the hardware store doesn't have an owner exactly. he just lives there. they put a bed in the back. they feed him. he greets every customer. he is in the town newspaper twice a year. his name is steve. nobody knows why he's named steve. when steve dies the town is going to fall apart. don't think about it. just enjoy the steve we have.

sunday. lazy day. didn't get out of bed until noon. read a whole novel cover to cover. ate toast in bed. the dog slept across my legs and i pretended i couldn't move. i needed this. i didn't realize how much i needed this. monday is coming but for now it isn't. for now there's just this. and that's enough.

good day today. did a load of laundry. walked to the corner and back. read for twenty minutes without falling asleep. these things would have been nothing two years ago. now they are a triumph. i'm not being dramatic. they actually are. you have to recalibrate.

the sound of the screen door slamming behind someone is a specific kind of summer sound. it means a person you love is on their way out to join you. it means iced tea is coming. it means the evening is officially beginning. it means home, in a way that's hard to articulate.

had a whole stitch-along with a friend on a video call tonight and we both got nothing done because we just talked the whole time but the embroidery was sort of the excuse for talking and i think that's the point of any craft circle in any era anywhere.

rainy day depression is real and so is rainy day joy and i can't always tell which one i'm in. today is one of the joy ones. i don't know what made it different. i'm sitting by the window with hot chocolate and reading and the dog is asleep at my feet and i feel like a soft animal in a soft world. it's not always like this. i'm going to enjoy it.

the kitchen is too small for both of us. but we do it anyway. i chop. you stir. we bump elbows. you say sorry. i say sorry. the rice cooker is on the floor because there's no counter space. the cat is judging us from the windowsill. dinner will be good. dinner is always good. that's how we know we made it.

this zine is for the girls who cry in target. this is for the boys who write poems in the notes app and never show anyone. this is for everyone who thinks they're too much and also somehow not enough. you are. and you aren't. and we love you here.

the corn from the farm stand is so sweet right now it's almost obscene. ate three ears on the porch with butter dripping down my wrists and didn't even care. there's a small window every year when corn is exactly this good. you miss it if you blink. i don't blink.

i think the best part of being a baker is that nobody knows what you've done by the time they walk through the door. they don't see the 4am turn or the temperatures or the proofing checks. they see bread. they see a glossy crust. they take it home and butter it. it's a very quiet kind of magic.

the wind has been coming off the lake for two days and the cabin sounds like a ship. the timbers creak. the windows hum. i sit by the fire and write and feel like a sailor in a story i haven't read yet. the wind doesn't care that i'm here. that's the comfort.

there's a baby behind me who has been screaming for forty minutes and the dad keeps apologizing to everyone and i keep saying it's okay even though it's not really okay, but it's also not the baby's fault, and it's not the dad's fault, and somehow this collective suffering is a kind of intimacy.

i'm trying to remember the name of the song that was playing in the car the night we drove home from the lake and i can hear the chorus in my head but i can't get to the words and it's been haunting me for three days and i refuse to look it up because if i find it that easily it won't mean anything anymore

i think about all the things i throw away every day and how each of them could have been part of something. it's a kind of mourning. not for the things themselves, but for the alternate universes where i was patient enough to save them, and made something good.

bought my first plant for the new apartment. a pothos. small. green. doing her best. i named her phyllis because she looks like a phyllis. i talk to her in the morning while i make coffee. nobody told me a plant would feel like a roommate but here we are.

the kitchen tile is the same kitchen tile that was in my grandmother's house and every time i walk on it barefoot i'm seven years old again and she's making sandwiches and the radio is on and the dog is sleeping under the table and i don't know any of the bad things yet and i can't tell if remembering this is comforting or devastating

my whole spice collection lives in a shoebox under the sink. labeled in sharpie. organized by which ones i actually use. cumin lives in the front. cardamom lives in the back. the bay leaves are in a ziplock. this is not how spice racks are supposed to work but it is how my spice rack works. and the food tastes the same.

made coffee on the woodstove this morning because the propane is out and i couldn't be bothered to drive the forty minutes into town for more. it took an hour. it was the best coffee of my life. i think most of modern life is just paying to skip the part where things take time.

she got married last summer and i couldn't go. i was sick. i hate that i couldn't go. she said it was okay. she sent me pictures. i cried looking at them. she looked so beautiful. her wife looked so happy. and i felt very far away. and i thought about the night i met her in 2008. and i thought about how much i love her. how much i still do.

couldn't sleep. been awake since 3. thinking too much. i know you're at work right now. don't text back. just wanted somewhere to put the words. i'm okay. just one of those nights. talk later. love you. go sell that house.

i tried to do a no-buy month and i lasted exactly nineteen days before i caved and bought a vintage lamp at a yard sale for eight dollars. i'm not even sorry. it has a little ceramic owl on the base. it brings me so much joy. i don't think i'm cut out for no-buy challenges. i'm more of a buy-less-stuff-thoughtfully person.

the trick to a small kitchen is doing things in order. wash everything as you go. don't dirty a bowl if you can use a measuring cup. cook with one pan if at all possible. accept that you will eat standing up. accept that you might eat directly out of the pan. the food will still be good. you will still feed yourself. that's the whole point.

i found the keys. they were in the freezer. don't ask. i don't know how they got there. but. found. crisis over. coming home now. love you. and yes i checked twice. they're definitely the right keys this time.

i forgot to call my mother on her birthday last year and i still think about it every single day and she said she didn't care but she did care and i know she did and i can't undo it and i call her every week now but it doesn't feel like enough and maybe nothing would feel like enough

she asked me to sign her yearbook and i wrote three sentences and erased them four times before settling on have a good summer with a smiley face. i was incapable of saying i love you i love you i love you. i still think about what i could have written. i still think about it twenty years later. that's how love works i guess.

i love that you laugh at your own jokes before you finish them. i love that you cry at sports movies. i love that you bring me coffee on saturdays before i'm awake and leave it on the bedside table where it gets cold. i love that you do that even though i never drink it cold. you keep trying. you keep loving me your way.

the older i get the more i think the secret to happiness is just having a couple of friends you can be ugly with. not pretty-ugly. ugly-ugly. the kind where you don't shower before they come over. the kind where you say the embarrassing thing first. that's it. that's the whole secret.

my favorite paperback has been water-damaged. i found it that way. someone had spilled tea on it years before i bought it. you can see the ring on the cover. and the pages are warped in the middle. and yet i love this copy more than any pristine copy would be. the damage is the history. the damage is what makes it mine.

we finally cleaned out the garage. found a box of letters my grandfather wrote to my grandmother during the war. they are unbelievably tender. they are unbelievably stupid in places. they are deeply themselves. i sat on the floor of the garage and read them for two hours. i cried twice. i'm glad we kept them. i'm so glad.

logged on to write about my day but i can't really remember it. i made coffee. i answered emails. i ate a sandwich at my desk. i went on a walk. i came home. nothing happened. and yet i'm exhausted. and yet i feel like i need to log this somewhere. proof that today existed. proof that i was here.

the camp had a chapel that nobody used except us. we'd sneak in at night and sit in the pews and tell each other secrets. i told them about my parents. they told me theirs. we were twelve. we didn't know how good we had it. we didn't know we'd never be that honest again. we thought everyone was like this. we thought this was just life.

the neighbor's cat has decided my porch is part of her territory and shows up every evening at 6:30 sharp expecting a small saucer of water and three minutes of attention. she has trained me. she's correct to do so. i have submitted to the routine.

the freedom to leave a dish in the sink for two days is something i did not know i would value this much. nobody has an opinion. nobody is silently judging. nobody is loudly judging. the dish is in the sink. it is my dish. it is my sink. i'll wash it when i want to.

no need to call back. just wanted to say i was thinking about that thing you told me last summer about your dad. i think you were right about it. i think it took me a year to understand what you meant. anyway. you're smarter than you give yourself credit for. love you. bye.

back from a week of being offline. i don't know what to report. i read three books. i ate breakfast outside every morning. i swam in cold water. i didn't think about anyone i'm supposed to be thinking about. i don't know if it changed anything. but i feel slightly more like myself. whatever that means.

found a used poetry collection that had a pressed flower between pages 47 and 48. it was a violet. it was so old it was the color of a bruise. i put it back exactly where i found it. i bought the book. now the violet lives between pages 47 and 48 in my apartment. i think about her. whoever pressed it. whatever she was reading. why she chose those pages.

found a sea glass in the tideline today, pale green, the color of old bottles. soft on every edge. it's been in the water for what, fifty years, eighty? something someone threw away long before i was born, polished smooth and given back to me. i don't believe in much but i believe in the sea making gifts.

the woman who runs the bookstore down the street has a face like an old painting. she's been there forty years. she remembers what every regular reads. she pulled a book off the shelf for me last week before i'd even said what i was looking for. she said i think you're ready for this one. i was. i don't know how she knew. she is in the business of knowing.

i keep meaning to write here more often and then days go by and nothing gets written. i think it's because the small things feel too small and the big things feel too big. there's no middle. but actually maybe the small things are the whole point. so. small thing. the dog got groomed today. she looks ridiculous. she's so proud. that's it. that's the entry.

the smell of a library is a mix of old paper and slightly damp carpet and whatever cleaning solution they use on the desks. i could pick it out blindfolded. it would make me feel safe even if you dropped me in the strangest city on earth, just to walk into a library and breathe in.

you can't outrun a sunday / no matter how fast you go / you can't outrun a sunday / you can't outrun yourself / the church bells are ringing / for nobody in particular / and i'm getting older / and the years are getting shorter / and i don't know what to do with my hands anymore

the host tonight wore a denim jacket with a pin that said 'be gentle with yourself' and she introduced every poet like they were her family. when she said my name she looked right at me and i felt twenty feet tall. there are people who hold a room together. she's one of them.

i don't own a stand mixer. i don't own a food processor. i don't own a kitchenaid anything. i own one good knife and a wooden spoon my mother gave me when i moved out at twenty-two. and you know what. the food is fine. the food is great. you don't need stuff to cook. you need to be hungry and unafraid.

i had a meeting with a stranger at a cafe today. she was an old friend of a friend. we sat across a small table and drank coffee and talked for three hours about everything. about her divorce. about my dead father. about the books we'd been reading. we walked out into the rain. we hugged. we'll probably never see each other again. and that was the whole point.

writing little notes on the white border under the photo with a fine-point pen so i don't forget. today at the diner. the second i knew. the cat in the window of the antique shop on 7th. these aren't captions, exactly. more like marginalia.

the first time we held hands in public i was twenty-six and i had never done it before. i had never been able to. and you didn't make a big deal of it. you just took my hand at the farmer's market like you'd been doing it your whole life. and i wanted to cry but i didn't. i smiled at the tomatoes instead. i held your hand. and we kept walking.

i found a stack of letters my grandmother wrote to my grandfather during the war. they are in her looping handwriting. they are addressed to him at a base in france. they smell faintly of an attic. she is asking him to come home. she is asking gently. she is asking like a woman who knows she has to wait. i can't read them all at once. i can only read one a day.

a film that ends with a static shot of a hallway for forty-five seconds is a film that respects you. it says here, sit with it, decide what you think. the hallway means whatever you bring to it. the hallway is the question. the credits roll. you go home. you think about the hallway for a week.

this series feels overworked to me. i can see every revision. every second-guess. every moment you almost gave up and kept going. that's not a compliment. the labor is showing through and it's drowning the image. step away. let the next one breathe. let yourself make something that isn't perfect on purpose.

if i die before my mother, the only thing i would want her to read is a letter i wrote her last december and never sent. it's in my desk. it says everything. it apologizes for things she doesn't know she's owed an apology for. it thanks her for things she doesn't know she gave me. i hope she reads it. or i hope i tell her instead. one of the two. preferably both.

race tomorrow. i'm not ready. i'm never ready. that's not the point. i ate pasta tonight. i laid out my clothes. i have my bib. i have my shoes. i have a small banana for the morning. now i'm going to lie awake until 3am thinking about every possible way the race could go wrong. that's also part of the training.

i wrote his name on the back of my math notebook in pencil so i could erase it if anyone asked. i practiced our combined initials. i looked up the meaning of his name in a book. i told nobody. nobody. it was the most important secret of my life. he didn't know i existed. it didn't matter. it absolutely didn't matter.

songs for driving alone at night when you have nowhere to be. songs for crying in the bathtub. songs for missing someone you shouldn't miss. songs for sitting in the parking lot of your old high school when you're back in town. songs for endings that don't feel like endings yet.

the back of my embroidery looks like a crime scene and the front looks like a polite garden and i think that's the most accurate metaphor for being a person that i've ever made by accident. presenting one side, hiding the chaos of the construction.

the fridge hums in that specific way it does at 2am, like it's keeping a secret. i'm eating cold spaghetti from the container with a fork that's slightly too big for the job. there's something about kitchens at this hour that feels like a different country. the tile is colder. the light from the open fridge does that yellow thing. my mother used to do this exact thing, i remember now, watching her shadow on the wall when i couldn't sleep as a kid. i guess we both ended up here.

love is / a small / wet / animal / that lives / under your / ribs / and you / feed it / and / sometimes / it / bites you / and / sometimes / it / sleeps / and you / can / almost / forget / it's / there

if i could write you one good song / i would write you one good song / about the way you laugh at jokes that aren't funny / about the way you hum when you're thinking / about the way you make me a person / who is worth being

first frost this morning. the basil is dead. the marigolds are clinging on. the dog refused to go outside until i bribed him with a piece of cheese. the kitchen smells like coffee and toast. i lit a candle even though it isn't dark yet. autumn is a religion in this house. you can't fight it.

my niece asked me today why i don't wear dresses. i said because i don't want to. she said that's a good reason. she's seven. she got it immediately. why do adults make this so complicated. why does anyone need a longer explanation. that's the explanation. that's the whole explanation.

dear twenty-year-old me. i know you think your roommate hates you. she actually has anxiety. she will tell you this in three years over coffee. she will apologize for being distant. you will both cry a little. you will become friends again. please don't write her off. please don't be so quick to assume.

dear six-year-old me. you are going to love so many things in your life. a black cat. a book about a horse. a song your aunt sings at thanksgiving. a small green dress. a creek behind a friend's house. you are going to be okay. i know things are loud at home. but you are going to be okay. i promise.

to the kid in my eighth grade english class who told me my poem was good. i don't remember your name. i don't think we ever talked again after that. but i'm a writer now and i think about that small kindness probably twice a year. it mattered. it really mattered. i hope you're doing well.

the pothos has taken over the entire bookshelf. it is now reaching toward the ceiling. i used to think i was the one in charge here. i was incorrect. the pothos lives here too. the pothos has opinions. the pothos is patient. one day i will come home and the pothos will be wearing my clothes. it's coming. i can feel it.

watched a movie tonight where almost nothing happened for an hour and then a woman cried in a kitchen for ten minutes and i thought it was the best film i've seen all year. that's what i want from indie cinema. people in rooms. the camera not moving. someone finally letting something out.

the goodwill on cedar had a soviet army surplus coat for thirty dollars. i bought it. it's enormous on me. it smells like a basement. i love it more than i love most things in my life. i am going to wear it through every winter until i die. it is now my coat. it was someone else's coat for sixty years. now it's mine.

i made this issue in two weeks of fevered productivity at my kitchen table. there's coffee on page seven. there's a fingerprint on page twelve. there are typos. i don't care. this is a handmade thing and handmade things have evidence of the hand. i hope you read it on a porch somewhere. i hope a moth lands on it.

watching towns go by from a bus window is one of the better drugs. you don't know anyone, no one knows you, you're a streak passing through. there's a guy mowing his lawn and he doesn't know you exist and you'll never see him again and somehow that's beautiful instead of sad.

weird how grief works. you'll be fine for months and then a stranger on the bus laughs the same way your grandmother did and suddenly you're nineteen again in her kitchen and she's still alive and the soup is still on the stove and nothing bad has happened yet.

we are knitting hats for the hospital this month. for the nicu. for the babies who come early. tiny hats. so small they fit on my fist. we have made forty-three so far. we want to make a hundred. we will probably make more. we are old women with time on our hands. our hands are useful. that is the point. our hands are still useful.

made a tiny collage today inside an altoid tin and gave it to my best friend for her birthday. she cried. i was not expecting her to cry. she put it on her bookshelf and now every time i visit she shows it to whoever else is over. there is no greater compliment for a small piece of art.

the bookstore on third has a cat who sleeps in the philosophy section. i go in just to visit the cat. i pick up a book. i pet the cat. i put the book back. i leave. i have done this for three years. i have never bought a book there. i feel guilty about it. last week i finally bought one. it was a children's book about a cat. she would have liked it.

this is a soundtrack for the first cold day of fall. for putting on a sweater that smells like last year. for staring out a window with a hot drink. for thinking about everyone you've loved. for being okay with the thinking. for letting the thinking be the whole point.

monday. trying to start over. new notebook. fresh page. that always feels good for about two weeks and then i lose track of it. but two weeks of writing is more than zero weeks. so. here we go again. hello journal. it's me. nothing's really different. but i'm trying. and that counts.

dear nine-year-old me. you were right about your gut feeling on miss carter. she really did not like you and it really wasn't your fault. you were not a bad kid. you were not weird. you were a fine kid. she was just tired and in the wrong job. you didn't deserve to be made to feel small. you deserved better.

to the barista at the cafe on 5th who knows my order and asks how my mom is doing: i don't know how you remember any of us. i know you have your own life. but the way you make me feel seen at 8am on a wednesday is the closest thing i have to going to church. thank you. you do good work.

started a new sampler tonight. just basic running stitch in this dusty pink dmc that i've been hoarding for like two years waiting for the right project. there's something so satisfying about the rhythm of it. needle up, needle down. the fabric pulled taut in the hoop. my cat watching like she might pounce but she never does, she's mostly given up on the embroidery floss as prey.

i wear vintage every day. people ask me why. the honest answer is that new clothes don't fit my body. they are made for a body i don't have. vintage was made when there were more body types. when sewing was custom. when nothing was meant to be one size fits all. vintage fits me because it was made before fits were mass produced. that's the secret.

the camera ate a pack of film today. i don't know why. she just refused to spit them out and when i opened the back to see what happened, i ruined the next two frames in the process. the polaroid is the only relationship in my life where i forgive this kind of behavior. it's part of the contract.

i don't think the lead actor was a real actor. i think she was the director's actual neighbor. and that's what made it work. the awkward pauses were her actual awkward pauses. you can't pay for that. you can only find it, and ask gently, and pray they say yes.

the new apprentice cried today over a tray of scones that came out flat and i remembered being 22 and standing exactly there. i told her about the time i scorched twelve loaves and slept under the prep table and woke up to my boss laughing at me. she laughed which is the entire point. you have to laugh at the bread eventually.

today miss thompson kept me after class to ask if everything was okay at home. i don't know what i did to make her ask. i said yes everything's fine. i don't know if she believed me. i'm not sure if everything is fine. but i'm not going to talk to a teacher about it. that's not what teachers are for. or maybe it is. i don't know.

made toast at midnight which i think is a love letter to yourself sometimes. butter melting into the holes. honey on top. ate it standing up over the sink so the crumbs would go somewhere acceptable. the cat watched me with that judgmental look she has but i think secretly she approves of small acts of self-care even when they look stupid.

her grandmother died last week. she called me at 3am her time because i was the only person awake. we talked for two hours. she cried. i didn't know what to say. i didn't have to say anything. she just needed someone on the line. i made tea while she talked. she could hear the kettle. she said it was comforting. it was the most useful i've been in a year.

the woman across the aisle is eating an entire rotisserie chicken with her bare hands and i have never respected anyone more in my life. she has a plastic bag for the bones. she has wet wipes. she has prepared. this is a woman who knows what a six hour bus ride requires.

my favorite thing to cook on bad days is rice and an egg. you put a little oil in a pan. you crack an egg. you let the edges go crispy. you put the egg on the rice. you add soy sauce. you add hot sauce. you eat it with a spoon. it costs almost nothing. it tastes like home. it tastes like being okay.

vintage cookbook from 1964. spiral bound. someone's handwritten notes in the margins. the previous owner liked her potatoes well-seasoned. she crossed out the salt amounts and wrote more more more in pencil. she also wrote her shopping list inside the back cover. flour, sugar, eggs, milk. it has been there for sixty years. i will not erase it. i will not.

the local art store charges fourteen dollars for what i can find on a single block of any street in this city if i walk slowly enough. the world is making art supplies all the time. you just have to be in the habit of looking down.

monday. didn't sleep well. the cat woke me at 4 and i couldn't get back. spent the morning irritable and trying to hide it from everyone. ate a yogurt. went for a walk at lunch. felt slightly better. tomorrow i'll go to bed earlier. that's the plan. that's always the plan.

the air conditioner here makes a low hum that is almost meditative. i think they tune libraries to a frequency that helps concentration. or maybe i'm just inventing that because it would explain why i can write here in a way i cannot write at home, where the silence is the wrong shape.

i wrote my book at a cafe over the course of three years. they let me sit there for hours and only buy one drink. they put a sign on the table eventually that said reserved for the writer. i didn't ask for the sign. it just appeared. i still don't know who put it there. i finished the book. they're in the acknowledgments. they don't know.

everyone on this bus is going somewhere with a whole life i'll never know about. the woman with the laminated bible. the kid with the skateboard. the older guy who keeps making phone calls in a language i can't place. we're a temporary collective. we'll never assemble like this again.

tonight at the corner cafe a girl in a yellow cardigan read a poem about her grandmother's hands and the entire room went so quiet you could hear the espresso machine three rooms back. she didn't look up once. she was reading it to her own shoes. but every single one of us was reading it with her.

today's collage is built around a movie ticket from a date that didn't go well and a leaf from the tree i sit under in the park. you can't tell looking at the finished piece what either thing meant. that's the point. the meaning is composted into the work.

we live in different time zones now but we keep a shared notes app where we write to each other when we think of something. she lives in melbourne. i live in chicago. we write little messages. a song. a recipe. a stupid thought. a bird we saw. we read them when we wake up. it's slower than texting. it's more like a letter. it's better.

i'm thinking about my grandmother who loved rain more than anyone i've ever known. she would open all the windows. she would sit by them and read. she said the smell of rain was her favorite smell. she said it smelled like beginnings. she was right. it does smell like beginnings. i never told her i thought she was right. she died nine years ago.

the new cafe opened on third street and i don't know how to feel about it. it's beautiful. the chairs are real wood. the cups are real ceramic. but it's expensive. and it's busy. and the old cafe one block away is going to close because of it. and i don't know which one i should go to. i think i have to choose. i think this is a moral question.

the city is quieter in the rain. the streets emptier. the people more wrapped up. i went for a walk under the umbrella my dad gave me ten years ago. it's losing one of the spokes. i should replace it. i won't. i'll keep walking under it until it falls apart. there are some objects you have to use until they're done. there are some objects that are a promise.

current wip: a tiny bowl of cherries on a piece of natural linen. they're going to be ridiculous and i love them already. i'm using six strands of red because i want them to look like cartoon cherries and not real cherries. art lies. that's the whole point.

the group meets every wednesday in the back room of the library. we have been meeting for six years. there are eight of us. two of us have died. we have not replaced them. their chairs are still there. nobody sits in them. we just leave them. we knit. we talk. we say their names sometimes. ann would have loved this yarn. judith hated this pattern. they are still with us. they are still in the room.

marjorie brought scones today. she does this once a month. they are slightly burned on the bottom. we eat them anyway. we tell her they are perfect. she pretends to believe us. nobody actually believes us. but we all play the game. that's part of the knitting circle. we lie about the scones. we tell the truth about everything else. it balances out.

we used to live in the same apartment when we were twenty-two. we ate every meal together. we slept on the same fold-out couch some nights when one of us was sad. and now she's in another country and we go months without talking and we pick it up again like nothing happened. that's the kind of friendship that survives oceans. that's the kind of friendship you don't realize you have until you're tested by distance.

i used to hate rain. i grew up somewhere it rained all the time. i wanted sun. i moved south. i got sun. and then i missed the rain. and now i live somewhere it rains again and i love it. i wasted years complaining about something that turned out to be one of my favorite things. i wonder how many other things i'm doing that to right now.

soft october sunday. coffee on the porch. the cat in the window. the leaves doing their slow yellow business. nothing to report. nothing to sell you. just a small life happening in real time. i think this is what they call contentment. i think i'm finally home.

the salvation army had a wedding dress for fifty dollars. it was beautiful. i don't need a wedding dress. i'm not getting married. i bought it anyway. i'm going to wear it in my apartment. i'm going to wear it while making dinner. i'm going to wear it because i can. wedding dresses are too beautiful to only wear once. that's not a thing i agreed to.

the boots came in the mail. they fit. they are heavier than i expected. they make me walk differently. they make me hold doors open. they make me carry things. i don't know if that's the boots or me but i like the version of myself who lives inside them. i'm not taking them off for a week.

the sound design in this one is incredible. you can hear refrigerators humming. you can hear someone unscrew a jar of pickles three rooms away. it's a film made by people who know that the world is mostly sound, and that you can build mood out of the gentle drone of a furnace.

the fiddle leaf fig is doing fine this week and i am refusing to celebrate because the moment i acknowledge it the plant will drop seventeen leaves out of spite. it has done this twice. it knows when i am happy. it cannot be allowed to know. we live in detente. i water it. i do not love it openly. it does not betray me.

the lake froze solid this week and you can hear it groan at night when the temperature drops. low boom sounds, like distant cannons. it's the ice shifting. it scared me the first time. now it sounds like a friend turning over in her sleep in the next room.

i am once again thinking about how the phrase i'll sleep when i'm dead is something only people who have not yet experienced really good sleep would say. sleep is the best thing. sleep is the point. i want to sleep so well that when i die i'll be disappointed i don't get to do it anymore.

pacing. pacing. pacing. the doctors keep saying it like a mantra. don't push through. stop before you have to stop. i used to be someone who finished things, who pushed through, who got tired in the middle and kept going. that person nearly killed me. learning to be the other person is its own job.

broken-up but not over it. that's the vibe. that's the entire vibe. songs that aren't about your ex specifically but feel like they were written about your ex specifically. songs you can't listen to in public because you'll start crying on the bus. songs that are kind of bad but you love them anyway.

there's a woman in the group who doesn't actually knit. she just comes for the conversation. she crochets. we tease her about it. she takes it well. she is the youngest of us. she is sixty-four. she calls us the elders. she is not wrong. we are. we are. we welcome her anyway. crocheters are also welcome here. we are not gatekeepers.

running with the dog today went sideways. she saw a squirrel at mile two. she pulled me off the trail. i fell. she sat down and looked at me like i was the one being unreasonable. i was bleeding from my elbow. she licked my face. i couldn't be mad. she's a dog. i'm the one who clipped her to my waist. i am the architect of my own pain.
